claim: The medial prefrontal cortex plays a key role in higher order cognitive functions like decision making and social cognition.
source: The medial prefrontal cortex plays a key role in higher order cognitive functions like decision making and social cognition.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Euston et al., 2012; Dias et al., 1996; Ray and Zald, 2012) as indicated in the manuscript.

claim: Fast-spiking interneurons control the timing of excitatory neuron firing via somatic inhibition.
source: Fast-spiking interneurons (FSIs) control the timing of excitatory neuron firing via somatic inhibition and generate gamma (30–100 Hz) oscillations.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about FSI function in the field.

claim: Fast-spiking interneurons generate gamma (30–100 Hz) oscillations.
source: Fast-spiking interneurons (FSIs) control the timing of excitatory neuron firing via somatic inhibition and generate gamma (30–100 Hz) oscillations.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about FSI function in the field.

claim: Serotonin acts via 5HT2A receptors to suppress an inward-rectifying potassium conductance in FSIs.
source: Here, we show that serotonin (5HT), which is known to regulate gamma power, acts via 5HT2A receptors to suppress an inward-rectifying potassium conductance in FSIs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 2 showing effects of 5HT and 5HT2A antagonists on FSI properties and potassium currents.

claim: Serotonin leads to depolarization of FSIs.
source: This leads to depolarization, increased input resistance, enhanced spiking, and slowed decay of excitatory post-synaptic potentials (EPSPs).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1 showing membrane potential changes with 5HT application.

claim: Serotonin leads to increased input resistance in FSIs.
source: This leads to depolarization, increased input resistance, enhanced spiking, and slowed decay of excitatory post-synaptic potentials (EPSPs).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1 showing input resistance changes with 5HT application.

claim: Serotonin leads to enhanced spiking in FSIs.
source: This leads to depolarization, increased input resistance, enhanced spiking, and slowed decay of excitatory post-synaptic potentials (EPSPs).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1 showing increased firing rates with 5HT application.

claim: Serotonin leads to slowed decay of excitatory post-synaptic potentials (EPSPs) in FSIs.
source: This leads to depolarization, increased input resistance, enhanced spiking, and slowed decay of excitatory post-synaptic potentials (EPSPs).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 1 and 5 showing increased EPSP decay time constants with 5HT application.

claim: Slowed EPSP decay preferentially enhanced temporal summation and firing elicited by gamma frequency inputs.
source: Notably, we found that slowed EPSP decay preferentially enhanced temporal summation and firing elicited by gamma frequency inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 5 and 7 showing frequency-specific enhancement of summation and spiking.

claim: Synchronized oscillations of neuronal activity in the gamma frequency range (30–100 Hz) play a key role in information encoding.
source: Synchronized oscillations of neuronal activity in the gamma frequency range (30–100 Hz) play a key role in information encoding (Buzsáki and Chrobak, 1995; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012) and prefrontal gamma oscillations influence the performance of tasks related to cognitive flexibility and attention (Cho et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Buzsáki and Chrobak, 1995; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012).

claim: Prefrontal gamma oscillations influence the performance of tasks related to cognitive flexibility and attention.
source: Synchronized oscillations of neuronal activity in the gamma frequency range (30–100 Hz) play a key role in information encoding (Buzsáki and Chrobak, 1995; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012) and prefrontal gamma oscillations influence the performance of tasks related to cognitive flexibility and attention (Cho et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Cho et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2016).

claim: Serotonin has been shown to regulate gamma power in motor cortex.
source: The neuromodulator serotonin (5HT) has been shown to regulate gamma power in motor cortex (Puig et al., 2010), suggesting that it could play a role in regulating task-dependent changes in gamma oscillations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Puig et al., 2010).

claim: Neuropsychiatric disease associated with deficits in PFC gamma synchrony, including schizophrenia and depression, are currently treated with medications that have high affinity for serotonin receptors.
source: Furthermore, neuropsychiatric disease associated with deficits in PFC gamma synchrony, including schizophrenia and depression, are currently treated with medications that have high affinity for serotonin receptors (Meltzer and Massey, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Meltzer and Massey, 2011).

claim: Gamma oscillations are orchestrated by cortical fast-spiking interneurons.
source: Gamma oscillations are orchestrated by cortical fast-spiking interneurons (FSIs; Cardin et al., 2009; Sohal et al., 2009; Bartos et al., 2007; Bartos et al., 2002; Galarreta and Hestrin, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Cardin et al., 2009; Sohal et al., 2009; Bartos et al., 2007; Bartos et al., 2002; Galarreta and Hestrin, 2001).

claim: FSIs resonate intrinsically in the 30–50 Hz range.
source: In contrast to neighboring excitatory cells, FSIs resonate intrinsically in the 30–50 Hz range (Bracci et al., 2003; Fellous et al., 2001; Pike et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Bracci et al., 2003; Fellous et al., 2001; Pike et al., 2000).

claim: FSIs are more likely to generate action potentials in response to gamma-modulated sinusoidal waveforms.
source: In turn, FSIs are more likely to generate action potentials in response to gamma-modulated sinusoidal waveforms (Pike et al., 2000), suggesting that action potential generation in FSIs may favor gamma frequency input.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Pike et al., 2000).

claim: 5HT can increase FSI intrinsic excitability, as measured at the soma.
source: Indeed, 5HT can increase FSI intrinsic excitability, as measured at the soma (Weber and Andrade, 2010; Zhou and Hablitz, 1999; Zhong and Yan, 2011), but whether this also changes how FSIs encode synaptic input is not known.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Weber and Andrade, 2010; Zhou and Hablitz, 1999; Zhong and Yan, 2011).

claim: 5HT consistently depolarized FSIs by 6.1 ± 1.1 mV, from −71 ± 1.3 mV to −66 ± 2.2 mV.
source: 5HT consistently depolarized FSIs by 6.1 ± 1.1 mV, from −71 ± 1.3 mV to −66 ± 2.2 mV (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, p<0.005, paired t-test 5HT vs. baseline, n = 10; Figure 1C, p=0.03, 5HT n = 10 vs. time-locked controls n = 8, post-hoc Tukey comparison after one-way ANOVA with p=0.005)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and Figure 1C with statistical analysis.

claim: 5HT increased input resistance by 31.1 ± 6.0%, from 92.9 ± 11.5 MΩ to 121.6 ± 16.9 MΩ.
source: and increased input resistance by 31.1 ± 6.0%, from 92.9 ± 11.5 MΩ to 121.6 ± 16.9 MΩ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, p=0.026, paired t-test 5HT vs. baseline, n = 10; Figure 1D, p=0.037 5HT n = 10 vs. time-locked controls n = 8, post-hoc Tukey comparison after one-way ANOVA with p=0.004).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and Figure 1D with statistical analysis.

claim: The concentration of 30 µM 5HT was sub-saturating, eliciting approximately 80% of the maximal response.
source: We found this concentration of 30 µM to be sub-saturating, eliciting approximately 80% of the maximal response (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 5HT depolarized FSIs even in the presence of ionotropic glutamatergic and GABAergic antagonists.
source: 5HT depolarized FSIs even in the presence of ionotropic glutamatergic (10 µM CNQX, 100 µM DL-AP5) and GABAergic (10 µM SR95531) antagonists (Figure 1C–D, p=0.043 for Vm and p=0.05 for Rin, 5HT + syn block n = 9 vs. time-locked controls n = 8, post-hoc Tukey comparison after one-way ANOVAs with p=0.005 for Vrest and p=0.004 for Rin)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D with statistical analysis.

claim: Effects of 5HT on FSI membrane potential and input resistance were blocked by the 5HT2A antagonist MDL100907.
source: but effects were blocked (n = 7) by the 5HT2A antagonist MDL100907 (1 µM, Figure 1C–D, p=0.024 for Vm and p=0.026 for Rin, 5HT vs. 5HT + 2A antagonist post-hoc Tukey comparison after one- way ANOVAs with p=0.005 for Vrest and p=0.004 for Rin).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D with statistical analysis.

claim: 5HT signals through 2A receptors expressed on FSIs.
source: Thus, 5HT signals through 2A receptors expressed on FSIs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that 5HT2A antagonist blocks 5HT effects.

claim: 5HT increased spiking in FSIs in response to somatic current injection.
source: Indeed, 5HT increased spiking in response to somatic current injection (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, p=0.028 for treatment factor, 5HT vs. baseline in repeated measures two-way ANOVA for firing rate vs. current curve with current and treatment as factors, n = 10; Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, p = 0.001, rheobase, 5HT vs. baseline, paired t-test, n = 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,F with statistical analysis.

claim: No other changes in intrinsic firing properties were noted after 5HT application.
source: No other changes in intrinsic firing properties were noted after 5HT application (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G-L.

claim: Two broad classes of cortical interneurons arise from the medial (MGE) and caudal (CGE) ganglionic eminences.
source: Two broad classes of cortical interneurons arise from the medial (MGE) and caudal (CGE) ganglionic eminences (Rudy et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Rudy et al., 2011).

claim: Interneuron classes that arise from the CGE, including CCK and VIP interneurons, express 5HT3A receptors exclusively.
source: Interneuron classes that arise from the CGE, including CCK and VIP interneurons, have been shown to express 5HT3A receptors exclusively (Lee et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Lee et al., 2010).

claim: Intrinsic excitability of somatostatin-expressing interneurons was unaltered by 5HT application.
source: Intrinsic excitability was unaltered by 5HT application (p=0.34 for Vm and p=0.14 for Rin, paired t-test 5HT vs. baseline, n = 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis on SOM+ neurons.

claim: FSIs respond to serotonin in a unique manner compared to other interneuron types.
source: Overall, this indicates that FSIs respond to serotonin in a unique manner.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential responses of FSIs and SOM+ interneurons to 5HT.

claim: Endogenous 5HT release increased FSI firing rate from 10.9 ± 3.8 Hz to 29.8 ± 6.8 Hz.
source: Endogenous 5HT release increased FSI firing rate from 10.9 ± 3.8 Hz to 29.8 ± 6.8 Hz (Figure 1F, p=0.035, during stimulation vs. before stimulation, paired t-test, n = 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F with statistical analysis using optogenetic stimulation of serotonergic terminals.

claim: The increase in FSI firing rate from endogenous 5HT release was blocked by the 5HT2AR antagonist MDL100907.
source: This increase was blocked by the 5HT2AR antagonist MDL100907 (Figure 1G, 1 µM, p=0.32, during stimulation vs. before stimulation, paired t-test, n = 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G with statistical analysis.

claim: 5HT application increased the number of spikes elicited by each light flash during optogenetic activation of glutamatergic inputs.
source: 5HT application increased the number of spikes elicited by each light flash (Figure 1G, p<0.0001 for both treatment and flash number in repeated measures two-way ANOVA, p<0.0001 for the interaction term, p<0.05 for flashes 1–8 5HT vs. baseline post-hoc comparison Bonferroni correction, n = 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G (note: text says 1G but likely refers to 1J based on figure) with statistical analysis.

claim: EPSP amplitude did not change with 5HT application during optogenetic stimulation.
source: Interestingly, EPSP amplitude did not change (Figure 1K, p=0.120, paired t-test 5HT vs. baseline, n = 7, Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1K with statistical analysis.

claim: EPSPs decayed more slowly following 5HT application, with decay tau increasing from 10.4 ± 1.2 ms to 17.4 ± 3.5 ms.
source: However, EPSPs decayed more slowly following 5HT application (Figure 1L, decay tau: baseline 10.4 ± 1.2 ms, 5HT: 17.4 ± 3.5 ms, p=0.037, same analysis, n = 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1L with statistical analysis.

claim: 5HT decreased the slope of the I-V curve in FSIs.
source: 5HT decreased the slope of the I-V curve (p=0.037, paired t-test 5HT vs. baseline, n = 7), indicating a decrease in membrane conductance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from voltage clamp recordings with statistical analysis.

claim: The current modulated by 5HT displayed inward rectification and reversed at −99 ± 4.7 mV.
source: This current displayed inward rectification and reversed at −99 ± 4.7 mV, very close to the predicted reversal potential for K+ in our preparation (−101 mV).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from voltage clamp recordings showing the reversal potential of the 5HT-sensitive current.

claim: The 5HT-mediated current and I-V curve slope change were abolished with pre-application of MDL100907.
source: Both the 5HT-mediated current (p=0.0007, KGluc +MDL100907 vs. KGluc, post-hoc Tukey multiple comparison test with one-way ANOVA with p<0.0001, Figure 2F) and I-V curve slope change (p=0.04, same analysis, Figure 2E) were abolished (n = 3) with pre-application of MDL100907 (1 µM) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B, E, F with statistical analysis.

claim: 5HT modulates an inward rectifying K+ channel in FSIs.
source: 5HT-sensitive currents reversed at potassium equilibrium and were smaller in the outward direction, suggesting that 5HT modulates an inward rectifying K+ channel.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing reversal potential and rectification properties of the 5HT-sensitive current.

claim: The 5HT-mediated current and changes in I-V curve were absent when using a cesium-based internal solution.
source: Both the 5HT-mediated current (p<0.0001, CsMe vs. KGluc, ANOVA with post-hoc Tukey multiple comparison test, Figure 2F) and changes in I-V curve (p=0.007, same analysis, Figure 2E) were absent (n = 6) in these conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C, E, F with statistical analysis using cesium-based internal solution to block K+ channels.

claim: The I-V curve changes and 5HT-mediated current were blocked by Ba+ at 400 µM.
source: Again, both the I-V curve changes (p<0.0001, BaCl2 vs. KGluc, ANOVA with post-hoc Tukey multiple comparison test, Figure 2E) and the 5HT-mediated current (p=0.01, same analysis, Figure 2F) were blocked (n = 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D, E, F with statistical analysis using Ba+ to block inward-rectifying K+ channels.

claim: 5HT reduces the conductance of inward rectifying potassium channels in FSIs.
source: Thus, 5HT reduces the conductance of inward rectifying potassium channels in FSIs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from voltage clamp experiments with various pharmacological manipulations.

claim: Reducing K+ conductance in a compartmental model of a fast-spiking interneuron increased Vm and Rin.
source: Reducing K+ conductance in a compartmental model of a fast-spiking interneuron (Figure 3A) also increased Vm and Rin (Figure 3B)
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: A reduction of gK by 60–70% across the cell was sufficient to recapitulate experimental data on Vm and Rin changes.
source: a reduction of gK by 60–70% across the cell was sufficient to recapitulate our experimental data.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results matching experimental observations.

claim: Only dendritic reduction of gK resulted in an increase in synaptic time constant in the computational model.
source: Indeed, when K+ channel conductance was systematically reduced in different subcompartments (Figure 3C soma only, Figure 3D dendrites only, Figure 3E both soma and dendrites), only dendritic reduction of gK resulted in an increase in synaptic time constant (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 3C-E, G.

claim: No manipulation of gK affected EPSP amplitude in the computational model.
source: Interestingly, consistent with our experimental observations during optogenetic stimulation of inputs to FSIs (Figure 1L), no manipulation of gK affected EPSP amplitude in our model (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Reducing dendritic gK to mimic 5HT caused a decrease in EPSP amplitude and synaptic current when measured at the dendrite.
source: In fact, in our compartmental model, reducing the dendritic gK to mimic the experimentally observed effects of 5HT on somatic Vm and Rin caused a decrease in the EPSP amplitude and synaptic current when measured at the dendrite (90% of baseline amplitude, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C)
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: The dendritic EPSP attenuates less as it travels toward the soma after reducing dendritic gK.
source: However, due to the increase in Rin, the dendritic EPSP also attenuates less as it travels toward the soma such that the EPSP amplitude, measured at the soma, is ultimately unchanged by this manipulation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from computational modeling results explaining why somatic EPSP amplitude remains unchanged despite dendritic changes.

claim: 5HT significantly increased FSI firing rate when applied immediately adjacent to a dendrite via iontophoresis.
source: 5HT significantly increased FSI firing rate when applied immediately adjacent to a dendrite (Figure 4B, p=0.001, before iontophoresis vs. after iontophoresis, paired t-test, n = 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B with statistical analysis using dendritic iontophoresis of 5HT.

claim: Dendritic iontophoresis of 5HT elicited a 1.19 ± 0.69 mV depolarization of the soma.
source: By computationally filtering out spikes from our traces, we determined that dendritic iontophoresis of 5HT elicited a 1.19 ± 0.69 mV depolarization of the soma (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: A somatic depolarization of 2.63 ± 1.57 mV of FSIs was sufficient to cause an increase in firing rate comparable to that observed by dendritic iontophoresis of 5HT.
source: By applying this same filtering technique to spike trains elicited by somatic current injection, we found that a somatic depolarization of 2.63 ± 1.57 mV of FSIs was sufficient to cause an increase in firing rate comparable to that observed by dendritic iontophoresis of 5HT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 5HT only increased firing rate when the iontophoretic pipette was <5 µm away from the dendrite.
source: By placing the iontophoretic pipette at varying distances from the dendrite, we determined that 5HT only increased firing rate when the pipette was <5 µm away (space constant = 3.13 µm, Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E with distance-dependent effects.

claim: All iontophoretic sites were >30 µm from the soma.
source: All iontophoretic sites were >30 µm from the soma (Figure 4E), confirming that effects are due to local action of 5HT at receptors on the dendrite and not due to diffusion of 5HT to the soma.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E documenting distances of iontophoretic sites from soma.

claim: 5HT did not affect single EPSP amplitude during glutamate uncaging experiments.
source: Consistent with ChR2 synaptic stimulation experiments (Figure 1H–L) and compartmental modeling (Figure 3), 5HT did not affect single EPSP amplitude (Figure 5C, p=0.45, normalized change in amplitude: Post/Pre, one-sample t-test vs. 1, n = 39 dendrites, 25 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C with statistical analysis using glutamate uncaging.

claim: 5HT increased the time constant of EPSPs from 14.7 ± 0.6 ms to 18.6 ± 1.0 ms during glutamate uncaging.
source: However, 5HT did increase the time constant of the EPSPs from 14.7 ± 0.6 ms to 18.6 ± 1.0 ms (Figure 5D, p=0.0002, change in tau: Post – Pre, one-sample t-test vs. 0, n = 39 dendrites, 25 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D with statistical analysis.

claim: Changes in EPSP decay peaked 10–20 ms after stimulation with 5HT.
source: As with ChR2 synaptic stimulation, changes in EPSP decay peaked 10–20 ms after stimulation (Figure 5E)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: 5HT significantly promoted summation at 10 ms inter-stimulus intervals during glutamate uncaging.
source: As predicted, 5HT significantly promoted summation, specifically at the 10 ms (p=0.05, change in fifth EPSP amplitude: 5HT/Baseline, one-sample t-test vs. 1, n = 26 dendrites, 18 cells; p=0.006, change in area under curve: 5HT/Baseline, one-sample t-test vs. 1, n = 26 dendrites, 18 cells, Figure 5H)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H with statistical analysis.

claim: 5HT significantly promoted summation at 20 ms inter-stimulus intervals during glutamate uncaging.
source: and 20 ms intervals (p<0.05, change in fifth EPSP amplitude, same analysis as above, n = 29 dendrites, 20 cells, Figure 5G; p=0.0171, change in area under curve, same analysis as above, n = 29 dendrites, 20 cells, Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G-H with statistical analysis.

claim: By slowing the decay of synaptic potentials, 5HT promotes summation of gamma frequency inputs.
source: Thus, by slowing the decay of synaptic potentials, 5HT promotes summation of gamma frequency inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from glutamate uncaging experiments showing frequency-specific enhancement of summation.

claim: Changing the synaptic time constant in an algebraic model promoted summation of inputs at 10–20 ms intervals more than other frequencies.
source: Consistent with experimental data, changing the tau of the EPSP decay promoted summation of inputs at 10–20 ms intervals more than other frequencies (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A 70% reduction in gK throughout the neuron changed Vm, Rin, and tau by an amount comparable to the experimental effect of 5HT.
source: A 70% reduction in gK throughout the neuron changed Vm, Rin, and tau by an amount comparable to the experimental effect of 5HT (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 6D comparing model and experimental results.

claim: In the compartmental model, the reduction in gK could reproduce the frequency-specific enhancement of summation observed in uncaging experiments.
source: Furthermore, in the model, the reduction in gK and resultant change in tau could reproduce the frequency-specific enhancement of summation observed in our uncaging experiments. Specifically, inputs arriving within 10–20 ms were summated preferentially, as compared to higher (0–5 ms ISI) or lower (50 ms ISI) frequencies.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results matching experimental observations of frequency-specific summation.

claim: Preferential summation at 10–20 ms ISIs was observed even when synaptic strength, synapse placement, or number of synapses were varied in the model.
source: Preferential summation at 10–20 ms ISIs was observed even when we varied synaptic strength, synapse placement on the dendritic arbor, or number of synapses recruited (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Even when Rin was reduced up to 33% by including background synaptic noise, summation remained tuned to enhancements for 10–20 ms in the model.
source: But even when Rin was reduced up to 33%, summation remained tuned to enhancements for 10–20 ms (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D with background synaptic noise.

claim: CNO application increased Vm in FSIs expressing the Gq-DREADD receptor.
source: However, in FSIs expressing the Gq-DREADD receptor, CNO application increased Vm (Figure 7C; p<0.0001, paired t-test CNO vs. baseline, n = 7)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C with statistical analysis using chemogenetic activation.

claim: CNO application increased Rin in FSIs expressing the Gq-DREADD receptor.
source: Rin (Figure 7D; p=0.0004, paired t-test CNO vs. baseline)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D with statistical analysis.

claim: CNO application increased spiking in FSIs expressing the Gq-DREADD receptor.
source: and spiking (Figure 7B) in FSIs
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: CNO application produced similar changes in Kir function as 5HT in FSIs expressing the Gq-DREADD receptor.
source: and produced similar changes in Kir function (Figure 7E), suggesting that hM3D receptors can co-opt signaling pathways downstream of 5HT2A receptors and mimic the effects of 5HT on FSI physiology.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E with voltage clamp recordings.

claim: hM3D receptors can co-opt signaling pathways downstream of 5HT2A receptors and mimic the effects of 5HT on FSI physiology.
source: suggesting that hM3D receptors can co-opt signaling pathways downstream of 5HT2A receptors and mimic the effects of 5HT on FSI physiology.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing similar effects of CNO on Gq-DREADD expressing FSIs as 5HT.

claim: CNO application mainly enhanced EPSPs following ISIs of 10 or 20 ms during electrical stimulation.
source: Interestingly, CNO application mainly enhanced EPSPs following ISIs of 10 or 20 ms (p=0.04 for 10 ms and p=0.046 for 20 ms, normalized change in EPSP integral: CNO/baseline, one sample t-test vs. 1, n = 7, Figure 7I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7I with statistical analysis.

claim: CNO increased the percentage of spikes that occurred after stimulation with 10 ms ISI compared to other frequencies.
source: Specifically, CNO increased the percentage of spikes that occurred after stimulation with 10 ms ISI compared to other frequencies (p<0.0001 for treatment in ANOVA, p=0.002 for 10 ms vs. 20 ms, p<0.0001 for 10 ms vs. 50 ms, p=0.004 for 10 ms vs. 100 ms, post-hoc comparison with Tukey's correction, Figure 7I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7I (note: text says 7I but likely refers to 7J based on figure) with statistical analysis.

claim: Effects on FSI Vm and Rin were similar with α-methyl-5HT as with endogenous 5HT and Gq-DREADD activation with CNO.
source: Effects on FSI Vm (p=0.002, paired t-test baseline vs. α-methyl-5HT, n = 5) and Rin (p=0.01, paired t-test baseline vs. α-methyl-5HT, n = 5) were similar with α-methyl-5HT as with endogenous 5HT and Gq-DREADD activation with CNO (Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Figure 7—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B-C with statistical analysis using a 5HT2A agonist.

claim: α-methyl-5HT did not change the amplitude of subthreshold EPSPs.
source: As in other experiments, we found that α-methyl-5HT did not change the amplitude (p=0.96, paired t-test baseline vs. α-methyl-5HT, n = 5, Figure 7—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 with statistical analysis.

claim: α-methyl-5HT increased the decay time of subthreshold EPSPs.
source: but did increase the decay time (p=0.03, paired t-test baseline vs. α-methyl-5HT, n = 5, Figure 7—figure supplement 2E) of subthreshold EPSPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2E with statistical analysis.

claim: 5HT2AR agonism increased the percentage of spikes that occurred after stimulation with 10 ms and 20 ms ISIs compared to other frequencies.
source: Furthermore, we replicated our earlier findings and found that 5HT2AR agonism increased the percentage of spikes that occurred after stimulation with 10 ms and 20 ms ISIs compared to other frequencies (p<0.001 for treatment in ANOVA, p=0.002 for 10 ms vs. 50 ms, p=0.002 for 10 ms vs. 100 ms, p=0.01 for 5 ms vs. 20 ms, p=0.002 for 20 ms vs. 50 ms and 100 ms post-hoc comparison with Tukey's correction, 6 cells, Figure 7—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2D with statistical analysis.

claim: Serotonergic signaling in FSIs specifically enhances the ability of these cells to respond to gamma-frequency input.
source: Thus, serotonergic signaling in FSIs seems to specifically enhance the ability of these cells to respond to gamma-frequency input.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing frequency-specific enhancement of FSI responses to gamma frequency inputs.

claim: CNO dramatically increased the number of IPSCs recorded in pyramidal neurons.
source: We found that CNO dramatically increased the number of IPSCs recorded (p=0.04 paired t-test CNO vs. baseline, 5 cells, Figure 8C), indicating an overall increase in inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C with statistical analysis recording IPSCs in pyramidal neurons.

claim: The frequency of IPSCs shifted toward inter-event intervals of 10–20 ms after CNO application.
source: Interestingly, we also found that the frequency of IPSCs shifted toward inter-event intervals of 10–20 ms (Figure 8D)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: 5HT increases gamma frequency inhibition in the prefrontal network.
source: Thus, we conclude that 5HT increases gamma frequency inhibition in the prefrontal network.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased probability of gamma frequency inhibitory events in pyramidal neurons after Gq-DREADD activation in FSIs.

claim: FSI dendrites tend to function more as passive filters compared to pyramidal cells.
source: Compared to neighboring pyramidal cells, which can respond to synaptic input with the generation of dendritic superlinearities (Stuart and Spruston, 2015), FSI dendrites tend to function more as passive filters (Abrahamsson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Stuart and Spruston, 2015; Abrahamsson et al., 2012).

claim: FSIs exhibit subthreshold resonance around 30 Hz.
source: FSIs also exhibit subthreshold resonance around 30 Hz (Bracci et al., 2003; Fellous et al., 2001; Pike et al., 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Bracci et al., 2003; Fellous et al., 2001; Pike et al., 2000).

claim: Membrane resonance in FSIs contributes to network gamma oscillations according to network models.
source: and network models show that this membrane resonance contributes to network gamma oscillations (Moca et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Moca et al., 2014).

claim: FSIs show enhanced firing in response to gamma frequency modulation of sinusoidal current injected into the soma.
source: Furthermore, FSIs show enhanced firing in response to gamma frequency modulation of sinusoidal current injected into the soma (Pike et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Pike et al., 2000).

claim: FSIs are able to precisely control the timing of spike discharges of large populations of cortical neurons.
source: With abundant reciprocal connections and highly divergent synapses onto principal pyramidal cells, FSIs are able to precisely control the timing of spike discharges of large populations of cortical neurons (Bartos et al., 2007; McBain and Fisahn, 2001; Tamás et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Bartos et al., 2007; McBain and Fisahn, 2001; Tamás et al., 2000).

claim: FSIs orchestrate network oscillations, specifically in the gamma frequency range.
source: These properties endow FSIs with the ability to orchestrate network oscillations (Cardin et al., 2009; Sohal et al., 2009), specifically in the gamma frequency range, which have been suggested to be important for information encoding (Buzsáki and Chrobak, 1995; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Cardin et al., 2009; Sohal et al., 2009; Buzsáki and Chrobak, 1995; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012).

claim: Electrical stimulation of the dorsal raphe increased and decreased the activity of distinct populations of FSIs in secondary motor cortex via 5HT2A and 5HT1A receptors, respectively.
source: A previous study (Puig et al., 2010) found that electrical stimulation of the dorsal raphe of rat both increased and decreased the activity of distinct populations of FSIs in secondary motor cortex via 5HT2A and 5HT1A receptors, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Puig et al., 2010).

claim: Blocking 5HT2ARs decreased the power of gamma oscillations in motor cortex.
source: Furthermore, this group found that blocking 5HT2ARs decreased the power of gamma oscillations, suggesting that 5HT2AR activation could contribute to increases in gamma oscillatory power.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Puig et al., 2010).

claim: 5HT receptors are expressed on pyramidal neurons in prefrontal cortex.
source: While we focus here on the role of 5HT on FSIs, 5HT receptors are also expressed on pyramidal neurons (Araneda and Andrade, 1991; Avesar and Gulledge, 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Araneda and Andrade, 1991; Avesar and Gulledge, 2012).

claim: 5HT receptors are expressed on 5HT3a-expressing interneurons, including VIP, CCK, and others.
source: and 5HT3a-expressing interneurons, including VIP, CCK, and others (Puig and Gulledge, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Puig and Gulledge, 2011).

claim: Prefrontal dysfunction is etiological to many major psychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia and depression.
source: Prefrontal dysfunction is etiological to many major psychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia and depression (Drevets et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Drevets et al., 2008).

claim: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) remain the most commonly used treatments for depression.
source: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) remain the most commonly used treatments for depression (Risch and Nemeroff, 1992; Willner, 1985)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Risch and Nemeroff, 1992; Willner, 1985).

claim: Second-generation antipsychotics used in schizophrenia block the 5HT2A receptor with high affinity.
source: and second-generation antipsychotics used in schizophrenia block the 5HT2A receptor with high affinity (Meltzer et al., 2003; Meltzer and Massey, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Meltzer et al., 2003; Meltzer and Massey, 2011).

claim: Classic hallucinogens such as lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) activate the 5HT2A receptor.
source: Classic hallucinogens such as lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) activate the 5HT2A receptor (Titeler et al., 1988), implicating it in psychosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Titeler et al., 1988).

claim: Patients with schizophrenia show lower levels of the 5HT2A receptor in PFC.
source: Additionally, patients with schizophrenia show lower levels of the 5HT2A receptor in PFC (Arora et al., 1991; Selvaraj et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Arora et al., 1991; Selvaraj et al., 2014).

claim: Impairments in FSI function and gamma rhythms may be involved in the pathophysiology of schizophrenia.
source: Impairments in FSI function and gamma rhythms may also be involved in the pathophysiolology of schizophrenia (Gonzalez-Burgos et al., 2010; Gonzalez-Burgos et al., 2015; Lewis et al., 2005; Uhlhaas and Singer, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Gonzalez-Burgos et al., 2010; Gonzalez-Burgos et al., 2015; Lewis et al., 2005; Uhlhaas and Singer, 2010).

claim: Optogenetic activation of FSIs at gamma frequency is able to rescue impairments in cognitive flexibility in mice that model key aspects of schizophrenia.
source: Previous work from our group showed that optogenetic activation of FSIs at gamma frequency is able to rescue impairments in cognitive flexibility in mice that model key aspects of schizophrenia (Cho et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Cho et al., 2015).

claim: Treatment with antipsychotic drugs that act on 5HT receptors can reduce gamma power.
source: Furthermore, treatment with antipsychotic drugs that act on 5HT receptors can reduce gamma power (Schulz et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Schulz et al., 2012).

claim: CNO had no effect on Vm or Rin in FSIs expressing only the control fluorophore.
source: CNO had no effect on Vm or Rin in FSIs expressing only the control fluorophore (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 as a control experiment.
